items.stem: Under the encomienda system, the Spanish Crown granted a colonist the right to demand labor and tribute from a Native community. In theory, what did the colonist owe the community in return?
options: (A) Christian instruction for the Native community.
(B) Full legal ownership of the community's farmland and water rights.
(C) A share of the silver mined at Potosí.
(D) Military protection against French colonists.
items.explanation: The encomienda was framed as an exchange: the colonist received Native labor and tribute, and in return was supposed to provide Christian teaching and protection. In practice the labor demands overwhelmed any instruction, but instruction was the official justification.

option_explanations.A: Right — Christian instruction was the theoretical justification for the grant.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the encomienda granted labor and tribute, not land ownership.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — Potosí silver flowed to the Crown and the world economy, not to Native communities.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — defense against the French was not part of the encomienda's terms.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Encomienda: 'Spanish grant giving a colonist the right to extract labor and tribute from Native communities, in theory in exchange for Christian instruction'

items.stem: Las Casas wrote the passage below to persuade the Spanish Crown to reform its colonial policies. How does that purpose shape the passage?

stimulus.text: Now the ultimate end and scope that incited the Spaniards to endeavor the Extirptaion and Desolation of this People, was Gold only; that thereby growing opulent in a short time, they might arrive at once at such Degrees and Dignities, as were no wayes consistent with their Persons. Finally, in one word, their Ambition and Avarice, than which the heart of Man never entertained greater...
stimulus.attribution: Bartolomé de las Casas, A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (originally published in Seville, 1552; this English translation, 1689). Text verbatim from Project Gutenberg EBook #20321 (italic markers removed).

options: (A) He praises the encomienda system as fundamentally fair and just.
(B) He argues that Native peoples possessed no rights whatsoever under Spain.
(C) He stresses Spanish greed and cruelty to make reform seem urgent.
(D) He avoids blaming any Spaniards so the Crown will not take offense.
items.explanation: Las Casas was writing as an advocate, not a neutral observer. By painting the colonists' motives as pure gold-lust and describing the results as 'extirpation,' he aimed to shock the Crown into action. Recognizing that purpose helps readers understand why the passage emphasizes the worst abuses.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the passage condemns the colonists' conduct; it does not praise the encomienda.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — Las Casas spent his career arguing that Native peoples did possess natural rights.
option_explanations.C: Right — an advocate for reform highlights the evils that reform must address.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the passage directly blames Spanish 'Ambition and Avarice.'

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Bartolomé de las Casas: 'the Dominican friar whose writings denounced Spanish cruelty and helped curb (but not end) Native enslavement'; u1.md §What the exam tests here — 'Las Casas and the Valladolid debate are perfect sourcing material'

items.stem: The New Laws of 1542, pushed by Bartolomé de las Casas, did which of the following?
options: (A) Abolished all forced labor in the Spanish Empire immediately.
(B) Gave Native leaders voting seats in the Spanish government.
(C) Transferred the encomienda from individual colonists to the Catholic Church.
(D) Limited the encomienda and forbade new grants of Native labor.
items.explanation: The New Laws were a reform, not an abolition. They restricted the encomienda system — limiting existing grants and banning new ones — which is why they count as a curb on the system rather than its end.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the laws limited the encomienda; they did not abolish all forced labor.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — nothing in the New Laws created Native representation in Spanish government.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the laws restricted grants; they did not hand the system to the Church.
option_explanations.D: Right — limiting the encomienda and forbidding new grants is exactly what the New Laws did.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — New Laws (1542): 'Spanish reforms, pushed by Las Casas, that limited the encomienda and forbade new grants of Native labor'

items.stem: After the New Laws limited the encomienda, Spain increasingly imported enslaved Africans under the asiento system. Which statement best describes what changed and what stayed the same in Spanish colonial labor?
options: (A) Forced labor ended and was replaced everywhere by free wage labor.
(B) Coerced labor continued, but shifted from Native peoples to enslaved Africans.
(C) The encomienda expanded because the New Laws were never enforced anywhere in the colonies.
(D) Spain abandoned its American colonies entirely for lack of workers.
items.explanation: This is a continuity-and-change pattern: the demand for coerced workers never went away, so the system adapted. What changed was who was forced to work — as Native labor became harder to exploit, enslaved Africans were imported to take their place.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — coerced labor did not end; it changed form.
option_explanations.B: Right — the coercion continued while its victims changed.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the New Laws did limit the encomienda; the shift to African slavery is the evidence.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — Spain kept its empire; it replaced the labor force rather than leaving.

items.fact_source: u1.md §The story — 'Spain kept the empire but began replacing Native forced labor with enslaved Africans, imported under the asiento system — a fateful shift'; u1.md §What the exam tests here — 'Labor systems over time — from encomienda to the New Laws to African slavery: coerced labor continues, but who is coerced changes'

items.stem: At Valladolid in 1550–1551, Las Casas debated Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda over whether Native peoples possessed natural rights and rational humanity. What is the historical significance of this debate?
options: (A) It shows the morality of conquest was openly contested in 1500s Spain.
(B) It immediately ended the encomienda system throughout the empire.
(C) It demonstrated that all Spaniards agreed the conquest was fully justified.
(D) It convinced Spain to abandon its American colonies for good.
items.explanation: The debate matters because it happened at all: at the height of Spain's empire, the Crown sponsored a formal argument about whether its conquests were just. That tells us conquest was controversial even among the conquerors — it was contested in its own time, not only by later historians.

option_explanations.A: Right — a formal Crown-sponsored debate proves the morality of empire was disputed in the 1500s.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the encomienda had already been limited by the New Laws, and the debate did not end it.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — the debate's existence proves disagreement, not agreement.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — Spain kept its empire for centuries after Valladolid.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Valladolid Debate (1550–1551): 'the formal dispute between Las Casas and Sepulveda over the rights and rational humanity of Native peoples'; u1.md §What the exam tests here — 'Conquest was contested at the time'

items.stem: In the passage below, Las Casas identifies which motive as the driving force behind the destruction of Native peoples?

stimulus.text: Finally, in one word, their Ambition and Avarice, than which the heart of Man never entertained greater, and the vast Wealth of those Regions; the Humility and Patience of the Inhabitants (which made their approach to these Lands more facil and easie) did much promote the business: Whom they so despicably contemned, that they treated them (I speak of things which I was an Eye Witness of, without the least fallacy) not as Beasts, which I cordially wished they would, but as the most abject dung and filth of the Earth...
stimulus.attribution: Bartolomé de las Casas, A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies (originally published in Seville, 1552; this English translation, 1689). Text verbatim from Project Gutenberg EBook #20321.

options: (A) A sincere desire to spread Christianity.
(B) Direct orders from the Spanish king to destroy Native communities.
(C) Self-defense against repeated Native attacks.
(D) Gold, and the ambition and greed for quick wealth and status.
items.explanation: Las Casas is explicit: 'the ultimate end... was Gold only,' pursued through 'Ambition and Avarice.' He argues the colonists wanted fast riches and the social rank that came with them, and treated Native peoples as obstacles to that wealth.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — Las Casas says the motive was gold and greed, not missionary zeal.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — he blames the colonists' avarice, not royal orders; the Crown later passed the reforming New Laws.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — he insists the Spaniards 'never received any injury from the Indians.'
option_explanations.D: Right — gold, ambition, and avarice are the motives he names.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Bartolomé de las Casas: 'writings denounced Spanish cruelty'

items.stem: This 18th-century casta painting is labeled 'De español e india, mestiza' — 'From a Spaniard and an Indigenous woman, a mestiza child.' What does this painting best illustrate about Spanish colonial society?

stimulus.image_caption: Casta painting labeled 'De español e india, mestiza' (From a Spaniard and an Indigenous woman, a mestiza child), 18th century.

options: (A) Spaniards and Native peoples never mixed or formed families with each other in the colonies.
(B) Colonial artists refused to depict mixed-ancestry families in their work.
(C) The colonial regime carefully classified people according to their ancestry.
(D) The casta system treated every child identically regardless of parentage.
items.explanation: Casta paintings exist because colonial society was organized around ancestry: each combination of parents produced a named category with legal and social consequences. Painting and labeling a 'mestiza' child shows how seriously the regime took classifying people by descent.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the painting itself depicts a mixed family, so mixing clearly occurred.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — casta paintings are precisely depictions of mixed families.
option_explanations.C: Right — the labeled categories show ancestry-based classification.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the whole point of the casta system was to treat people differently by ancestry.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — 'Mestizaje and the casta system — racial mixing in Spanish America and the elaborate legal hierarchy that ranked people by ancestry'

items.stem: This 18th-century casta painting is labeled 'De negra y español sale mulato' — 'From a Black woman and a Spaniard comes a mulatto child.' What does this label reveal about the casta system?

stimulus.image_caption: Anonymous 18th-century casta painting labeled 'De negra y español sale mulato' (From a Black woman and a Spaniard comes a mulatto child).

options: (A) The system classified only people of Spanish and Indigenous ancestry.
(B) The system also classified the children of enslaved Africans, assigning them a named place.
(C) The system abolished slavery for all children of mixed ancestry.
(D) Spanish law prohibited any classification of African-descended people anywhere in the colonies.
items.explanation: The casta system covered everyone in the colonies, including the growing population of African descent. A 'mulato' label shows that children of African and Spanish parents were also sorted into the ancestry hierarchy — the system's reach extended to the enslaved population and their descendants.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — this painting classifies African-Spanish parentage, not Indigenous.
option_explanations.B: Right — the mulato category shows the hierarchy included people of African descent.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — classification did not abolish slavery or change anyone's legal bondage.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the painting itself is a classification of an African-descended child.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — 'Mestizaje and the casta system — racial mixing in Spanish America and the elaborate legal hierarchy that ranked people by ancestry'

items.stem: This casta painting labels the child 'cambujo,' the offspring of a mulatto father and a 'china' (mixed-ancestry) mother — one of dozens of such precise labels. The existence of so many specific categories is best understood as evidence of which colonial concern?

stimulus.image_caption: Anonymous 18th-century casta painting labeled 'De mulato y china sale cambujo' (From a mulatto and a china comes a cambujo child).

options: (A) The drive to fix each person's legal and social status by ancestry, even as mixing continued.
(B) A scientific program to study human biology and heredity in the colonies, sponsored by the Crown.
(C) Proof that colonial racial categories were stable, fixed, and never changed over time.
(D) An official campaign to eliminate all racial distinctions in colonial society.
items.explanation: The labels multiplied because reality kept outrunning them: people continued to mix, so the system kept inventing new names to pin everyone down. Dozens of categories show a regime anxious to classify a population that would not stay within neat boundaries.

option_explanations.A: Right — ever-finer labels show the effort to fix status by ancestry amid ongoing mixing.
option_explanations.B: Wrong — the categories served legal and social hierarchy, not science.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — multiplying categories show the system straining, not standing still.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — the paintings created distinctions; they did not eliminate them.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — 'the elaborate legal hierarchy that ranked people by ancestry'

items.stem: The asiento system is best described as which of the following?
options: (A) The famous 1494 treaty that divided the entire non-European world between Spain and Portugal.
(B) The Spanish Crown's monopoly contract for supplying enslaved Africans to Spanish America.
(C) A religious vow taken by missionaries serving in New Mexico.
(D) A system of elected town councils governing the Spanish colonies.
items.explanation: As Spain shifted from Native to African forced labor, it needed a steady supply of enslaved people. The asiento was the Crown's solution: a monopoly contract granting one party the exclusive right to ship enslaved Africans to Spanish America.

option_explanations.A: Wrong — the division of the Americas was the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494).
option_explanations.B: Right — the asiento was the monopoly contract for the African slave supply.
option_explanations.C: Wrong — missionaries took vows, but 'asiento' was a commercial monopoly, not a vow.
option_explanations.D: Wrong — town councils (cabildos) were a different institution entirely.

items.fact_source: u1.md §Key terms — Asiento system: 'the Spanish monopoly contract for supplying enslaved Africans to the Americas'
